slides.title: Design patterns: make the next change safer
keyPoints: 22 named patterns, one problem-solving method
Follow code, calls, ownership, and lifetime
Dr. Charles Dorner
slides.narration: Welcome to Design Patterns. Our job is to learn how to choose and defend an arrangement of code when a real requirement makes the current arrangement hard to change. A design pattern is a named solution structure for a recurring kind of problem. It is not a prize for using more classes. Throughout this course we will begin with working code, expose a specific limit, and then test a better arrangement. You will read C++ and diagrams together, predict what the program does, and explain what must remain true. Class 0 gives us the words and habits that make those later lessons useful.
actions: Open presenter notes for the spoken teaching script.

question.prompt: What evidence makes a pattern worth introducing?
question.answer: A concrete requirement exposes a change or failure that the new arrangement makes easier to handle while preserving the program’s promises.

slides.title: What counts as understanding a pattern?
keyPoints: State its pressure before its name
Locate roles in actual C++
Predict success and failure paths
Reject the pattern when a simpler design fits
slides.narration: Knowing the name is the first step, not the final test. By the end of a chapter you should be able to describe the problem in ordinary words, identify each responsibility in code, and follow a request through the objects that take part. You should also explain a failure case and an alternative design. The strongest test is a changed requirement: can you place the change without breaking earlier behavior? A class diagram can look familiar while the code fails its contract. We will therefore treat names, diagrams, output, and tests as parts of one explanation, rather than four separate lists to memorize.

slides.title: Pattern, algorithm, and library are different things
keyPoints: Algorithm: steps that compute a result
Pattern: responsibilities and relationships
Library: reusable implementation code
slides.narration: Imagine that a monitor must choose either an average or the highest reading. The steps for finding an average form an algorithm. The arrangement that lets the monitor use different algorithms through the same request may be Strategy. A standard library container, such as std::vector, is actual reusable code that stores the readings. These three things can appear in one program without meaning the same thing. A pattern does not give you a ready-made function to paste into every project. You must still choose data types, ownership rules, failure behavior, and tests that fit your program. That adaptation is where design judgment enters.

question.prompt: Does using std::vector mean that a program uses the Strategy pattern?
question.answer: No. A container supplies code for storing values. Strategy concerns making a varying operation interchangeable behind an agreed request.

slides.title: Start with one requirement and one function
keyPoints: Two readings are known to lie from 0 through 1000
Report their integer mean
No interchangeable object is needed
slides.narration: Our first requirement is deliberately small. Two integer readings lie between zero and one thousand, and the program reports their integer mean. Integer division drops any fractional part, which is acceptable for this demonstration. The values two and eight therefore produce five. A function with two parameters is enough. Each parameter is a local value initialized from an argument at the call. The return statement gives the result back to main. We have no evidence yet that creating interfaces or rule objects would help. A clear precondition, a small calculation, and an exact output make this design easy to review.
actions: Predict the output before running the complete program.
Change the inputs to 3 and 8 and explain why the result becomes 5.

question.prompt: What prints, and what assumption makes adding the two integers safe here?
question.answer: mean=5. Both inputs are restricted to 0 through 1000, so their sum is comfortably within the int range required by C++.

slides.title: A new requirement creates a design question
keyPoints: Some users need the highest reading
They must choose the rule during a run
Two stable branches may still be enough
slides.narration: Now users ask for the highest reading as well as the mean. That is a new requirement, not proof that the first function was badly written. For two stable choices, a small branch in one place can remain the best design. The pressure becomes stronger when several clients copy those branches, when rules change independently, or when a running program must replace its rule. Notice the order of our reasoning. We name the variation first: the estimate calculation. Then we ask where that variation currently spreads. Only after that do we compare a function parameter, an enum with a switch, and separate rule objects.

question.prompt: Which question should come first: “Which pattern?” or “What must vary independently?”
question.answer: Ask what must vary independently. That identifies the pressure and gives a reason to compare particular patterns.

slides.title: A safe demonstration of duplicated decision logic
keyPoints: Dashboard and report both select a calculation
Only one caller learns about the highest rule
The program compiles but the answers disagree
slides.narration: This program has no dangling pointer and no mysterious crash. Its failure is easier to miss: two callers interpret the same request differently. The dashboard handles the highest rule, but the report still always computes the mean. For readings one and nine, the reviewed dashboard prints nine while the stale report prints five. Both calculations are valid C++, so compilation cannot identify the missing requirement. Keeping one shared function would already repair this small case. If independently replaceable rules become a lasting need, a Strategy boundary can keep both callers from owning their own copies of the rule-selection logic.
actions: Ask learners whether the compiler should reject this program.

question.prompt: Why does the stale report print 5 instead of 9?
question.answer: It ignores the requested rule and always uses the mean calculation. The missing highest branch is a behavioral defect, not a syntax error.

slides.title: Judge a boundary by the change it contains
keyPoints: Keep rule calculations together
Make callers depend on one meaningful request
Pay for extra structure only when it earns its place
slides.narration: A boundary is the point where one part of a program meets another through a defined agreement. In our estimate example, a good boundary says what inputs the calculation accepts and what result it returns. The dashboard should not need to know every step of every calculation. However, a boundary does not always need a base class. One shared function could remove the duplicated logic today. A function parameter could let a caller supply a calculation tomorrow. A virtual interface becomes useful when named rule objects, stored choices, or lifetime management matter. We compare these costs against real changes, not against a rule that advanced syntax is always better.

slides.title: The creation family asks who builds the object
keyPoints: Factory Method: vary one creation step
Abstract Factory: create compatible families
Builder, Prototype, Singleton: different creation pressures
slides.narration: The five creational patterns organize object creation. Factory Method lets a shared workflow ask a replaceable creation step for the object it needs. Abstract Factory keeps a family of related choices compatible. Builder makes a multi-step construction process clearer. Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing configuration with a stated copy policy. Singleton controls access to one instance, which also creates concerns about shared state and lifetime. These names do not describe five spellings of new. Each addresses a different pressure. During the chapters, we will ask what must be created, who decides its exact kind, and who owns the completed result.

question.prompt: Why is “I need to create an object” too broad to select a creational pattern?
question.answer: All ordinary programs create objects. Selection depends on the particular pressure: a varying step, compatible family, staged construction, copying policy, or controlled instance.

slides.title: The structure family asks how parts fit together
keyPoints: Adapter translates; Bridge separates independent dimensions
Composite represents a tree; Decorator wraps behavior
Facade simplifies; Flyweight shares; Proxy controls access
slides.narration: The seven structural patterns organize how parts connect. Adapter changes the form of a request or value so two sides can work together. Bridge separates two dimensions that must vary independently. Composite treats a tree of parts through a common operation. Decorator adds behavior around another object. Facade offers a simpler entrance to a subsystem. Flyweight shares suitable common data. Proxy stands in front of another object to control access. Some of these diagrams contain a field that refers to another object, but that shared shape does not make the patterns identical. We must ask what the connection is for and what the caller is promised.

question.prompt: Adapter and Decorator can both hold another object. What separates their purposes?
question.answer: Adapter translates an interface or representation. Decorator preserves an interface while adding behavior around the wrapped operation.

slides.title: The behavior family asks how work is shared
keyPoints: Route, record, traverse, coordinate, or remember work
Notify, switch state behavior, or replace an algorithm
Fix a workflow or add operations across a type family
slides.narration: The ten behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. Chain of Responsibility routes requests along possible handlers. Command turns a request into something the program can store or schedule. Iterator traverses a collection without exposing its storage details. Mediator coordinates participants. Memento records restorable state. Observer notifies interested parties. State delegates behavior that depends on the current state. Strategy replaces an algorithm. Template Method fixes a workflow while allowing selected steps to vary. Visitor places related operations over a type family. You do not need to memorize every mechanism now. Keep the problem verbs as retrieval cues, then replace each short description with a code trace as we study the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter follows a chain of evidence
keyPoints: Requirement → baseline → limitation
Mechanism → code → predicted output
Failure → repair → justified alternative
slides.narration: We will use the same learning process while changing the problems. First, state a requirement and its limits. Next, make the simplest reasonable version and identify a specific new need it cannot handle well. Then introduce the feature or pattern that addresses that limit. Follow the actual code and diagrams, predict output, and run checks. Finally, break one promise deliberately, repair it, and compare a plausible alternative. This sequence prevents a common mistake: learning a pattern as a diagram detached from its reason to exist. When you review, practice retelling that chain in your own words before looking at the chapter answer.

slides.title: A type is a rule; an object is a particular instance
keyPoints: Class: a user-defined type
Object: one instance with a lifetime
Member: data or a function declared inside the class
slides.narration: A type tells the compiler what kind of value we are using and which operations are allowed. A class is one way to define a type that groups data and functions. An object is a particular instance of a type: two monitors can use the same class while holding different readings. A member belongs to the class declaration; a member function is often called a method. Object lifetime is the period in which that particular object exists, from completed construction until destruction begins. Pattern diagrams usually show types, but a running program contains objects. Keep that difference in mind when a diagram shows one rule box and execution creates several rule instances.

question.prompt: Does one Rule class box mean only one Rule object can exist?
question.answer: No. The box normally represents a type or role. Many objects can have that type, each with its own lifetime and state.

slides.title: A value parameter and a reference do different jobs
keyPoints: Value parameter: work on a separate parameter object
Reference: another name for an existing object
const reference: a borrowed view that cannot modify through that name
slides.narration: This example shows a mistake without causing unsafe memory access. add_to_copy receives a Tally value, so its change affects a separate parameter object. The tally in main remains five. add_to_original receives Tally followed by an ampersand, which declares a reference. The parameter is another name for the object in main, so adding three changes that object to eight. observe takes a const reference: it reads the same object while disallowing ordinary modification through that parameter. None of these calls transfers ownership. The original tally stays alive in main for all three calls, which makes the borrowed references valid.

question.prompt: Why are the printed counts 5 and then 8?
question.answer: The first function changes a value copy. The second changes the original through a reference. Both observations read the original tally.

slides.title: An invariant is a rule the boundary must preserve
keyPoints: Example: every monitor always has a usable rule
Private data blocks uncontrolled access
Every public operation must keep the rule true
slides.narration: An invariant is a rule that must remain true whenever a caller can observe the object at its public boundary. Suppose a monitor requires a usable estimate rule. Making its rule field private prevents ordinary outside code from directly clearing that field, but privacy alone is not enough. A public replace operation could still accept an empty owner and break the promise. A sound operation checks the proposed replacement before changing the current one. Encapsulation means placing related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. The point is to make valid changes easy and invalid states hard to create, not merely to add the word private.

question.prompt: A private rule pointer can be set to null by a public setter. Is the non-null invariant protected?
question.answer: No. Access control hides the field, but the public operation still allows a state that violates the contract.

slides.title: An interface includes promises, not just names
keyPoints: Precondition: what must hold before a call
Postcondition: what the call guarantees afterward
Invariant: what remains true at observable boundaries
slides.narration: An interface is the set of operations a caller may use together with the promises that give those operations meaning. An estimate function might require a nonempty list and guarantee a result within the range of its inputs. The nonempty rule is a precondition. The result guarantee is a postcondition. A permanently usable rule can be an object invariant. C++ function declarations describe types, but many of these value rules need written documentation and running checks. A function named estimate that silently returns Fahrenheit when callers expect Celsius can have the correct signature and still break the interface. Design begins with meaning before it becomes syntax.

question.prompt: Two implementations have identical signatures. Are they automatically interchangeable?
question.answer: No. They must also preserve the same preconditions, result guarantees, units, lifetime assumptions, and other promised behavior.

slides.title: One request, two implementations
keyPoints: Estimate defines the common request
Mean and Highest provide different behavior
The owner can replace its rule between calls
slides.narration: Here the new requirement finally earns an interchangeable rule. Estimate declares a virtual operation named value. Mean and Highest supply concrete answers with the same input contract: integers from zero through one thousand. The owning pointer initially holds Mean, so the first call returns five for one and nine. Replacing it with Highest destroys the old owned rule and makes the next call return nine. Both calls use the same expression, rule followed by an arrow and value. Virtual dispatch selects the implementation associated with the actual object during execution. This small program demonstrates the mechanism that the Strategy chapter will examine in depth.

slides.title: Read virtual, override, and const where they matter
keyPoints: virtual: permit dispatch through the base interface
override: ask the compiler to check the match
= 0: leave the operation abstract
const after the parameters: restrict changes through this call
slides.narration: In the preceding program, virtual marks a member function whose final override can be selected through a base reference or pointer. The equals zero after the declaration makes the operation pure virtual: Estimate does not provide a usable concrete answer there. Mean and Highest use override so the compiler rejects a mismatch with the base virtual function. The const after the parameter list applies to the receiving object through that call. It does not prove that the function has no possible outside effects. The colon in class Mean followed by public Estimate declares public inheritance. Here it means that a Mean can be used through the Estimate contract.

slides.title: Access, ownership, and lifetime are separate facts
keyPoints: A pointer can give access without owning
unique_ptr has one owner of its object
A borrowed reference does not extend the target’s lifetime
slides.narration: Ownership means responsibility for ending a resource’s lifetime. A raw pointer can hold an address without saying who owns the object. A reference gives access to an existing object but does not normally keep it alive. In our rule demo, unique_ptr is an owning handle that releases the concrete rule when replaced or destroyed. The virtual destructor in Estimate lets deletion through the base pointer reach the derived object correctly. These are distinct questions: who can call the object, who controls its release, and how long will it remain alive? Many pattern bugs occur when a diagram explains calls but leaves ownership and lifetime unstated.

question.prompt: Can storing a reference to a local rule keep that rule alive after its function returns?
question.answer: No. The reference does not extend that local object’s lifetime. Later use would be invalid unless the design keeps the target alive by another means.

slides.title: Move transfers a resource only through a move operation
keyPoints: std::move permits moving; it does not itself transfer
Moving unique_ptr transfers its owned object
The source unique_ptr becomes empty
Do not generalize that empty-state rule to every type
slides.narration: The expression std::move is best read as permission to treat an object as a source for moving. The move constructor or move assignment that receives it performs the actual transfer. When a unique_ptr is moved successfully, the destination becomes the owner and the source becomes empty. That specific rule lets us trace ownership without inventing a second object. Other moved-from library objects have different guarantees, so do not assume that every moved-from value is empty. A design that keeps using the source must respect its documented state. Later patterns use moves to hand completed objects to their caller without copying exclusive owners.

question.prompt: Does writing std::move(owner) on its own necessarily change owner?
question.answer: No. std::move is a cast-like operation that permits a move. A receiving move operation must perform the transfer.

slides.title: Read a range loop without guessing about punctuation
keyPoints: for visits each element in a range
The colon means “take each element from”
auto infers a type; & borrows; const restricts that access
slides.narration: When you see for followed by const auto ampersand child, a colon, and children, read it as: for each element in children, use a const reference named child. The colon belongs to the range-based for syntax. auto asks the compiler to infer the type; the ampersand avoids making an element copy; const limits modification through that reference. A const unique_ptr still permits changes to the pointed-to object unless the pointed-to type itself is const. Punctuation gets its meaning from context. A colon after a constructor’s parameter list instead begins member initialization, while a colon in a class declaration can introduce base classes.

slides.title: Separate what varies from what stays stable
keyPoints: Cohesion: related work belongs together
Coupling: parts rely on an agreement
Isolate evidence of change before creating an extension point
slides.narration: Cohesion asks whether the work inside one part belongs together. Coupling asks how strongly parts rely on each other. Neither word means that a program should contain isolated objects that never communicate. Our estimate callers must agree on inputs and results. The useful aim is a small, clear agreement that changes less often than its implementations. If report colors change for different reasons than temperature calculations, separating those responsibilities can reduce accidental edits. But guessing ten future variants may produce more complexity than the current task needs. Look for repeated edits, duplicated decisions, or a stated need to replace behavior before introducing an extension boundary.

question.prompt: What evidence would justify separating report formatting from alert calculation?

slides.title: Composition keeps independent choices independent
keyPoints: A report has a delivery collaborator
Two report types × three deliveries need not become six subclasses
Inheritance still fits a true substitution promise
slides.narration: Suppose two report formats can each use three delivery methods. A subclass for every pair leads to six combinations, and adding a fourth delivery creates more combinations again. Composition connects a report to a delivery object so each choice can vary separately. In broad design advice, composition can include borrowing a collaborator; in a strict UML composition relationship, the whole also controls its parts’ lifetime. We must therefore inspect the actual ownership rule. Inheritance remains useful when a derived type keeps a base contract or varies a step in a stable workflow. The goal is to match relationships to requirements, not to ban one C++ feature.

question.prompt: Why can composition reduce the number of combined types in the report example?
question.answer: It represents format and delivery as separate choices that are connected at use time, rather than defining a subclass for every pair.

slides.title: Single responsibility means one coherent source of change
keyPoints: Alert policy changes for one reason
Report appearance changes for another
One method per class is not the rule
slides.narration: The Single Responsibility Principle asks us to keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module might be a class or a source file. In our monitor, the alert rule answers whether a reading counts as an alert. A report formatter decides how accepted records appear on screen. A new workshop policy and a new color scheme come from different needs, so combining them can cause unrelated edits and tests to interfere. The principle does not mean every class should have exactly one function. A well-focused class may need several operations to protect the same data and fulfill the same responsibility.

question.prompt: Would moving every method into a separate class automatically satisfy single responsibility?
question.answer: No. Responsibility is about coherent reasons for change, not a numeric limit on methods.

slides.title: Open/closed protects a planned direction of change
keyPoints: Keep the monitor’s estimate call stable
Add another implementation for a new rule
Selection code still needs to choose the new rule
slides.narration: The Open/Closed Principle asks whether a known extension can be added without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. If the monitor calls an Estimate interface, adding another rule can leave its call site unchanged. Some construction or configuration code must still choose the new implementation, and that is acceptable. Closed does not mean no source file may ever change. It means a useful boundary protects one expected direction of change. Fixing a defect or changing the meaning of accepted input may still require editing that boundary. For a tiny fixed set of rules, a direct branch can be clearer than paying for an extension structure nobody needs.

slides.title: Substitution is a behavioral promise
keyPoints: A derived type must accept the base’s valid requests
It must keep the base’s result guarantees
Matching C++ syntax is necessary but insufficient
slides.narration: The Liskov Substitution Principle concerns what happens when a caller uses a derived object through a base contract. Suppose Estimate promises to accept every nonempty list of readings in a stated range. A derived implementation that secretly requires ten readings breaks that promise by strengthening the precondition. slides.title: Interface segregation follows the caller’s real needs
keyPoints: A reader should not require save or erase
Separate meaningful capabilities
Avoid creating dozens of empty one-method types
slides.narration: The Interface Segregation Principle asks whether callers depend on operations they do not need. An archive reader needs a load operation. If its only available interface also requires save, erase, and network setup, a read-only implementation may have to invent fake operations or throw surprising errors. Splitting reading from writing gives each caller a meaningful promise. One implementation can still support both capabilities. The aim is not the maximum number of tiny interfaces. Excessive splitting can hide which operations belong together. Start by naming the caller’s task, then group the operations needed to complete that task with a clear shared contract.

slides.title: Dependency inversion protects policy from detail
keyPoints: Policy: decide when an alert is needed
Detail: deliver it to a file or test buffer
Both depend on an appropriate alert-sink contract
slides.narration: The Dependency Inversion Principle concerns the direction of source dependencies. High-level policy says what the program must achieve. A low-level detail says how a device, file, or service carries it out. If alert policy directly depends on a particular file writer, file-format details can spread into the policy. An AlertSink contract can describe the delivery behavior policy needs. The policy depends on that contract, and a file sink or test sink implements it. The contract should express the policy’s need rather than expose every option of one file library. This makes a test implementation possible without making the domain decision about a physical file.

slides.title: Injection supplies a collaborator; inversion chooses the dependency
keyPoints: Constructor injection means receiving a needed object
A supplied concrete file writer is still a concrete dependency
The two ideas can work together but are not synonyms
slides.narration: Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside instead of constructing it secretly inside the consumer. A constructor parameter is a common way to do this. However, receiving a concrete FileWriter by reference is still a dependency on FileWriter. It is injection, but it does not automatically create dependency inversion. To judge inversion, look at the declared types and what those types promise. A policy receiving an AlertSink can depend on the abstraction while a composition site chooses the actual file sink. That composition site is allowed to know the concrete types because selecting and connecting them is its job.

keyPoints: Hollow triangle points toward a base type

slides.narration: A UML class diagram describes types and relationships, not a sequence of calls. In these lessons a solid line with a hollow triangle points from a derived type toward its base. A dashed dependency arrow says that one part uses another. It does not imply ownership. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of a composition relationship. A hollow diamond represents aggregation, but by itself does not specify who deletes a C++ object. Some lesson legends explicitly annotate shared ownership; confirm that claim against the actual owning handles. slides.title: Choose the diagram that answers the question
keyPoints: Activity: which branch or action comes next?
Sequence: who calls whom, in time order?
State: which changes are permitted?
Ownership: which event ends an object’s lifetime?
slides.narration: One diagram cannot answer every question equally well. An activity diagram follows possible actions and decisions; its arrows mean execution flow. A sequence diagram puts participants across the page and calls in order down the page. A state diagram shows permitted changes between named states after events. An ownership view makes owners, borrowers, and release events visible. A state diagram does not prove that a program uses the State design pattern: an enum and checked functions can implement the same transition rules. slides.title: Trace data, control, ownership, and lifetime separately
keyPoints: Data: arguments, stored values, results
Control: calls, branches, returns
Ownership: responsibility transferred or retained
Lifetime: construction and destruction events
slides.narration: A single call can move control without moving ownership. In the estimate demo, main passes two integer values to the selected rule; the result comes back by value. Control enters the rule’s override and returns to main. The unique_ptr remains the owner throughout that call. Replacement is different: it changes which rule is owned and destroys the old one. Lifetime ends at destruction, not merely when an arrow in a call diagram returns. Following these four paths separately prevents the common mistake of assuming that a caller owns every object it uses or that a returned reference keeps its target alive.

slides.title: Compilation and execution establish different facts
keyPoints: Compile: syntax, access, type compatibility
Link: required definitions can be resolved
Run: values follow the required behavior
A successful build is evidence, not a correctness proof
slides.narration: Compilation checks names, syntax, access rules, and many type relationships. It can reject an override whose signature does not match the base operation. Linking combines compiled pieces and may fail when a required definition is missing. Execution chooses branches for actual values, creates objects, calls functions, and destroys them. The stale report demo passes the build stages yet gives the wrong answer for the highest request. A virtual call’s required behavior is runtime selection of the final override, even when optimization can determine the target earlier. Keep the evidence precise: a successful build proves that this toolchain accepted the program, not that the program meets every requirement.

slides.title: Tests should challenge the promise, not just the happy path
keyPoints: Check ordinary inputs and exact outputs
Check boundaries and rejected requests
Verify state is unchanged after promised rejection

slides.narration: A test is most useful when it can catch a plausible incorrect implementation. A replacement test should check both before and after the change. A rejection test should verify not only that an error appears, but also that any promised unchanged state really stays unchanged. Where ownership matters, observe a real destruction event with a valid lifetime-safe test. These checks provide evidence for the cases they cover. They do not prove every possible execution, every allocator failure, or every platform behavior.

An algorithm is a set of steps that computes a result, such as finding the largest number. A pattern describes how responsibilities fit together, such as letting a caller choose among several algorithms. A library supplies usable code. A pattern supplies an idea that you must adapt. Strategy becomes useful when we want those rules to change independently. The extra objects have a cost, so two stable branches may still be the better choice.

slides.title: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose
keyPoints: Good design makes required behavior clear and likely changes manageable. Cohesion means keeping closely related work together. Coupling means how strongly one part relies on another. A useful design often raises cohesion and limits unnecessary coupling. There is no useful rule that all coupling must disappear: cooperating parts must agree on something. Aim for a small, stable agreement that a reader can explain and a test can check.

A useful design often raises cohesion and limits unnecessary coupling. There is no useful rule that all coupling must disappear: cooperating parts must agree on something. Aim for a small, stable agreement that a reader can explain and a test can check.

Encapsulate what varies. If new output styles keep changing a report calculation, separate formatting from calculation. The stable calculation can produce a result while a formatter chooses its presentation. First identify evidence of change: repeated edits, duplicated branches, or different user needs. Do not build a framework for a variation nobody needs. A function parameter may isolate the variation before a family of classes is worth its cost.

Program to an interface. A job that needs to store a result should ask for the storage behavior it needs, rather than reach into one particular file writer. The caller depends on a promise; implementations fulfill that promise. This permits a test implementation that keeps results in memory. It does not mean every class needs a separate interface. If there is one small, stable implementation, calling it directly can be clearer.

Favor composition over inheritance when separate choices must vary independently. With two report types and three delivery methods, making a subclass for every pair leads to six combinations. Connecting a report object to a delivery object keeps the choices separate. Inheritance still fits a true substitution relationship and a stable shared workflow. The question is which arrangement matches the change, not which language feature sounds more advanced.

slides.title: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design
keyPoints: Single Responsibility Principle: keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module is a part of a program that we can discuss as a unit, often a class or file. Suppose one class both decides which readings count as alerts and writes a color report. New alert policy and new report styling come from different needs. Separating those jobs lets each change without disturbing the other. This principle does not mean one function per class or one method per object.
slides.narration:
Single Responsibility Principle: keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module is a part of a program that we can discuss as a unit, often a class or file. Suppose one class both decides which readings count as alerts and writes a color report. New alert policy and new report styling come from different needs. Separating those jobs lets each change without disturbing the other. This principle does not mean one function per class or one method per object.

Open/Closed Principle: allow a planned kind of extension without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. Suppose the monitor validates readings and then asks an Estimate for a result. Adding a Median implementation can preserve that monitor code. The program still needs code or configuration that selects Median. "Closed" does not mean never fixing a bug or never changing a requirement. It means protecting a useful boundary from a known direction of change. A small fixed set of choices may need no extension boundary.

Liskov Substitution Principle: a derived type must keep the promises callers rely on from its base type. If Estimate accepts every nonempty list of values from 0 through 1000, an implementation that secretly requires at least ten values breaks that promise. It has strengthened a precondition, a condition required before a call. Returning a value outside a promised range weakens a postcondition, a guarantee after the call. Derived types must also preserve the base invariants. Test every implementation against the same contract, including small and boundary inputs.

Liskov substitution concerns behavior as well as legal C++ syntax. A method can compile with override and still return the wrong units or reject a valid request. Replacing a base parameter type with a different type normally does not override the function in C++; matching the required signature matters. Do not confuse the broad idea of accepting more cases with permission to change a C++ override signature. The compiler checks part of the contract; tests and review check the rest.

Interface Segregation Principle: a caller should not have to depend on operations it does not use. Suppose a small archive reader needs only load(), but its interface also requires save(), erase(), and network setup. A read-only implementation then needs fake operations or surprising failures. Split the meaningful capabilities so a reader depends on reading. One implementation may support several capabilities. Do not split every method into its own interface: the goal is a useful contract for each caller, not the largest possible number of types.

Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level policy and low-level detail should depend on suitable abstractions; the abstraction should not depend on the detail. High-level policy is the rule that says what the program must achieve. Low-level detail is how a device, file, or service carries it out. Let an alert policy depend on an AlertSink promise. A file sink and a test sink implement that promise. Changing the file format then need not change the alert decision.

Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside, often through a constructor. It can help implement dependency inversion, but the ideas are different. Passing a concrete file writer into a constructor is injection; policy can still depend directly on that writer. For inversion, inspect the types and their promises. SOLID principles help you ask questions. They are not five gates that force every small program to grow more classes.

TextRecord and BracketRecord provide choices in Chapter 1. A class body is inside braces, and the final semicolon ends the class declaration. public: marks members that callers may use. C++ has no separate interface keyword; an abstract class can express an interface.

Line by line: class Record begins the type. public: opens its public part. virtual ~Record() = default declares a virtual destructor and asks the compiler to supply its normal implementation. A destructor performs cleanup when an object is destroyed; the tilde marks its name. Virtual destruction makes deleting a derived record through the base pointer used by its owner safe. The format declaration returns a std::string, the standard library text type, and receives text as its input. The closing brace and semicolon finish the type.

In const std::string& text, the ampersand declares a reference: another name for an existing string, rather than a new string copy. const prevents changing that string through this reference. It does not promise that no other alias can change the same object. A value parameter would instead hold its own parameter object. The const after format(...) limits ordinary changes to the receiving object through that call. These two uses of const apply to different things.

virtual enables selection of an implementation through a base pointer or reference at run time. The = 0 marks a pure virtual function: this class leaves the operation to a derived implementation and cannot itself be instantiated. In a derived class, override asks the compiler to check that a function really overrides a base virtual function. final can prevent further derivation or overriding. Neither word proves the behavior is correct.

In Record* p, the star declares a pointer that holds an address and may be null. In *p, it follows the pointer to the object; a bad pointer makes that unsafe. p->format(text) calls a member through a pointer; a direct object uses a dot. A raw pointer does not state ownership. std::unique_ptr<Record> is an owning handle whose destructor releases its object. It permits one owner and cannot be copied. std::make_unique<TextRecord>() creates an object and returns its owner.

std::move(x) allows a move operation to be chosen; it does not itself move any object. Moving a unique_ptr into another owner transfers its object and leaves that particular source pointer empty. Do not assume all moved-from library objects are empty. The angle brackets in std::vector<int> or std::unique_ptr<Record> supply types to a library template, a reusable type recipe. You need to read these uses before you need to write templates.

In for (const auto& child : children), the colon means "take each element from children." auto asks the compiler to infer the element type; & borrows each element; const prevents changing that element through child. For a const unique_ptr this does not make the pointed-to object const. In a constructor, : member(value) instead starts member initialization. Context decides what the colon means. #include brings declarations from a header, std:: names the standard namespace, return supplies a result, and // starts a comment to the end of the line.

A UML class diagram shows types and their relationships. A solid line ending in a hollow triangle points from a derived class toward its base. A dashed line with an ordinary arrow shows a dependency. An association uses a solid line; an arrow, when present, shows navigable access. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of composition; a hollow diamond marks aggregation. A realization of an interface may use a dashed line with a hollow triangle. Read each page legend because line styles carry different meanings.

An activity diagram follows actions and decisions. Its arrows show possible execution flow, not inheritance. A sequence diagram places participants across the page and calls downward through time. A state diagram shows states and permitted transitions caused by events. An ownership view names owners, borrowed links, and the events that end lifetimes. Teaching links connect notes to code blocks; they are labeled annotations and are not UML relationships.

Compilation checks source syntax and many type rules, then produces code that the linker combines into a program. Missing definitions may fail at link time. Execution creates objects, selects branches, calls functions, and destroys objects. override errors can be caught during compilation. Choosing a valid but wrong strategy is an execution problem. Virtual calls preserve the required behavior of selecting the final override; a compiler may optimize how it achieves that behavior.

Trace four paths separately. Data moves as arguments and results. Control moves through calls and returns. Ownership moves only when the code transfers responsibility. Lifetime begins with successful object construction and ends with destruction. A borrowed reference does not keep an object alive. A retained pointer can outlive its target unless the design prevents that. In each chapter, ask who creates each object, who may call it, who releases it, and which tests cover those promises.

keyPoints: A reviewer says a class compiles with override, so it must satisfy the base contract. What should the team conclude?
slides.narration:
A reviewer says a class compiles with override, so it must satisfy the base contract. What should the team conclude?

Open Scenarios to select an answer and compare the reasoning for all four choices.

Ownership is automatically shared.. override says nothing about who owns an object.

Virtual calls always create new objects.. Dispatch selects a function implementation; it does not imply allocation.

Every valid input must now be accepted.. The compiler does not prove all preconditions are preserved.

The signature matches, but behavior still needs review and tests.. override checks an overriding relationship, not every input, result, or lifetime promise.

slides.title: Application case 2
keyPoints: A small program has two fixed output choices and one switch. No extension requirement exists. What is the strongest design decision?
slides.narration:
A small program has two fixed output choices and one switch. No extension requirement exists. What is the strongest design decision?

Open Scenarios to select an answer and compare the reasoning for all four choices.

Add a hierarchy for each choice immediately.. More types alone do not solve an observed limitation.

Use every creational pattern to future-proof it.. Unneeded extension points add maintenance work.

Remove the tests because the program is small.. A simple implementation still needs correct behavior.

Keep the direct design while testing its contract.. A pattern earns its cost by addressing a real source of variation.
